name: Ledger tooling
summary: Connecting AI agents to an accounting ledger through the Model Context Protocol.
insight: Give the agent a ledger, not a spreadsheet export.
body: An agent working from an exported spreadsheet is working from a photograph. Through a protocol server it can query the ledger itself: accounts, invoices, bank transactions, payroll. I maintain a fork of the open-source Xero MCP server, where my changes include Australian payroll tools and stricter input validation, and I package recurring accounting procedures as reusable agent skills.
The model is the least interesting part of that arrangement. The procedure and the permissions are where the quality comes from.
lessons: Read by default, draft by exception. An agent that can look at everything and post nothing is useful on day one and cannot make a mess.
Validate every identifier before it reaches a query. An ID that must be a GUID should be checked as a GUID, because model output is untrusted input.
Write the procedure down as a skill. A reconciliation that lives in someone's head cannot be delegated to a person or to a model.

name: AFK
summary: A workflow that lets an AI coding agent work unattended and still hand back something a reviewer can trust.
insight: An agent grading its own homework is not review.
body: Getting an agent to write code is the easy part. The hard part is knowing when the work is finished. AFK packages a delivery sequence as a plugin for coding agents: design, tests, implementation, internal review, review by a different model, the full test suite, then handoff. A draft pull request is a checkpoint in that sequence, never the end of it.
It works across agent hosts, and nothing about the project it runs in is written back into the plugin.
lessons: Independence beats capability. A reviewer from a different model family finds what the author could not notice, in the same way an auditor is useful because they did not prepare the accounts.
A finding is a hypothesis until someone demonstrates the consequence. Requiring evidence before a fix is what stops review from turning into churn.
State belongs outside the conversation. A run keeps a ledger of scope, decisions and open findings, so a new session can pick the work up without guessing.

name: MQT
summary: A personal research and trading platform for US equities, written in Python.
body: MQT covers market data, strategy analysis, risk controls, portfolio monitoring and audit logs. Language models do the reading and the analysis. They do not hold the keys: position limits, stops and order rules are ordinary code that a model's output passes through and cannot rewrite.
The repository is private and no strategy is published here. What transfers is the structure.
lessons: Put the model where a wrong answer is cheap and a good answer is valuable. Research is that place. Order placement is not.
Run new ideas in shadow before they touch money. A change that has only ever been right in a backtest has not been tested.
Log every decision with the inputs that produced it. The morning-after review is where the system actually improves, and it needs the evidence.

name: Nestli
summary: A baby-tracking app for iOS and Android, built and launched end to end.
insight: Shipping to a store is a different discipline from building a demo.
body: I owned the whole of it: product, mobile app, backend, data, the AI features, testing and the store releases. AI assistance is what made that scope possible for one person.
It also moved the bottleneck. Writing the code stopped being the slow part. Deciding what to build, and proving that it works on a real phone with a poor connection, became the work.
lessons: The unhappy paths are the product. Loading, empty, offline and error states are most of what a tired parent actually meets.
One person can build across the stack with AI. One person still has to verify across the stack, and that part does not get faster by itself.
A release process is a control. Store review and versioning do for an app what a close checklist does for a set of books.
